# Questions a reviewer is likely to ask

**How accurate is the range, and at what distances?** On the Mid-Air test flights (synthetic, so the truth is exact), the terrain-from-motion method has a median distance error of 3.1% (95 % interval 2.0% to 5.0%), with 91% of estimates valid, but one estimate in ten is more than 53% off. A flat ground plane with a take-off altimeter, the simple approach, has a median error of 315%. On real footage (AU-AIR) there is no ground truth, so only repeatability is measured: stationary vehicles' positions repeat to 7.6% of their distance. Ranges tested are short (low-altitude flight); no long-range claim is made. Evidence: `results/midair/test/terrain/`, `results/auair/repeatability_view_held_out_B2_yolo26n_960.json`.

**What happens near the horizon?** Errors grow quickly as the line of sight flattens. Below 2° of depression, error propagation becomes non-linear (the Monte Carlo prediction is 10.2 times the first-order one), and on AU-AIR the repeatability worsens from 5.8% of range at 20-40° to 10.6% below 10°. Rays at or above the horizon are reported as invalid, never ranged. Evidence: `results/midair/test/propagation.json`, D-517.

**Does it work on slopes?** A flat plane does not: its error grows from 6.4% on slopes under 5° to 23.7% above 45°. Terrain from motion builds a local ground surface from tracked image features and the drone's known motion. Its error stays between 1.9% and 3.7% on slopes up to 45°, and rises to 10.3% on slopes over 45° (still well below the flat plane there). Evidence: `results/midair/test/slope.json`, `results/midair/test/terrain/binned.json`.

**Is the uncertainty honest, and how do you know?** Not fully. The error bars were checked against the truth on flights not used to fit them: after calibration (split conformal prediction, fitted on separate calibration flights), nominal 68 %, 90 % and 95 % intervals contain the truth 63%, 84% and 90% of the time, against 74% for 90 % before calibration. So they are close but still a little over-confident on the test flights. Evidence: `results/midair/test/terrain/calibration.json`, D-403.

**What does the reliability flag catch and miss?** It is a small logistic model on interpretable features (local ground roughness relative to range is the strongest). On test flights its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) is 0.68: it flags 56% of the estimates that are more than 10 % wrong, and 45% of what it flags is wrong by that much. The large errors it does not flag are the rest, so it is a useful warning, not a guarantee. Evidence: `results/midair/test/terrain/flag.json`, D-404.

**What assumptions does the camera model make on real footage?** AU-AIR publishes no camera calibration. The focal length (1259 pixels) was measured from the drone's GPS motion against image motion on calibration flights and checked against car sizes; the principal point is assumed at the image centre; lens distortion is handled by using the central image only where it matters; the camera tilt is not recorded, so it is estimated from image motion (and checked against the visible horizon); the altimeter's zero drifts and was corrected where it could be measured. All of this is in `docs/auair_camera_model.md`.

**What latency, on what hardware, at what percentile?** On a laptop AMD Ryzen 7 5700U with Radeon Graphics CPU, the most accurate setting runs at 9.6 frames per second (103 ms per frame, median). The fast setting sustains 33.4 frames per second by running detection on every second frame and overlapping detection with tracking; each frame's result then arrives 47 ms after it is read (median; 99th percentile 77 ms). Evidence: `results/edge/pareto.json`, `results/edge/figures/pareto.png`.

**How was test data kept separate from tuning?** Every dataset has a split decided before results were seen (`results/splits.json`, D-506). Test splits ran once with `--final` after the settings were frozen; `scripts/freeze.py` recorded the hash of every setting file and the test queues stopped if any changed. Code fixes made during a test run (a crash on an empty result) changed no setting and are recorded (D-607). Evidence: `results/frozen/`, `docs/decisions.md`.

**Why not use a laser rangefinder or radar, and how would this combine with one?** This project asks how far a passive camera alone can go, and how honestly it can report its own uncertainty. An active sensor measures range far better; the natural combination is to use the camera for detection, tracking and bearing, and the rangefinder for range, with this pipeline's per-object uncertainty used to weight the two in the same Kalman filter, or to take over when the active sensor drops out.

**What would you do differently with real sensor telemetry?** Record the camera tilt and lens calibration (they had to be inferred here), use a properly referenced altitude (the altimeter drifted by metres within a flight), time-stamp camera and flight data together, and use a terrain model where one exists. Each would remove one of the largest error sources measured here.

**What is the weakest part of this work?** On real footage there is no ground truth for range or speed, so the real-footage results are repeatability and plausibility only, and 11% of vehicle speeds are implausibly high. On the tracking side, small people are rarely tracked (16% at 16 to 32 pixels). And 30 frames per second is reached only in throughput, at a cost in accuracy, not in per-frame delay.
